question: Should early-stage business development meetings be done virtually to protect your time, or in person because that is what actually converts?

sides.position: Do first and early meetings by video or phone — the two-hour coffee buys nothing a 30-minute call cannot, and refusing virtual is short-sighted.
Get in the room — proprietary funnel data shows in-person first interactions convert roughly 5x on management meetings and 10x on LOIs, and no amount of call volume substitutes.

why_it_matters: This decides how a business developer spends the scarcest resource they have: whether to run twelve video calls a week from a desk or four city visits, and whether a firm funds travel budgets at all.

evidence.speaker: AD
evidence.quote: I believe and one of the things I’ve really embraced post-COVID or since video conferencing has been introduced is, I don’t believe I will have an introduction face to face meeting again.

evidence.speaker: JR
evidence.quote: But that initial is a 30-minute phone or Zoom call. Pre-pandemic, that would be a coffee meeting or a lunch, which was no less than an hour, right?

evidence.speaker: EA
evidence.quote: While people hate — a lot of people I know in my role say, “I hate Zoom. You’ll never see me doing a virtual event again.” One, that’s short-sided and stupid.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: we were nearly five times more likely to go to a management presentation on a deal that we sourced out on the road in a city meeting, than over a phone call.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: you’re 10 times more likely to submit a letter of intent on a deal that was sourced during during a city visit versus a call, four times more likely to submit one, those sorts of the conference.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: Number two, it’s really the only time that’s free of distraction, at least for me.

caveat: Madsen is measuring private equity deal origination, where the counterparty has live transactions to allocate; Drost, Ries and Ackerman are talking about introductory relationship meetings in professional services where nothing is on the table yet. Madsen also concedes phone and video have a place between road trips, and Klein reserves in-person for closing.

question: Is business development in a professional services firm actually sales — to be named, processed and trained as such — or is calling it sales the thing that breaks it?

sides.position: It is sales, the aversion to the word is unfounded, and it should be run like sales — a documented process with defined steps, conversion ratios and ongoing training.
Drop the sales frame entirely — the job is helping and serving, and professionals who think of themselves as salespeople either freeze or get seen through by sophisticated clients.

why_it_matters: A firm leader either buys sales training and installs a pipeline process with accountability, or invests in relationship and leadership skills and deliberately removes sales language from how the firm talks about growth.

evidence.speaker: GB
evidence.quote: I go, “Congratulations, you’re in sales.” I mean, that’s really what it is.

evidence.speaker: RM
evidence.quote: Fundamentally, that first call you have with a prospective client. For us, we call a qualification call. I’ve broken the thing down into all the requisite steps.

evidence.speaker: AK
evidence.quote: I tell people all the time, “You know what? Then don’t ever use the word. Don’t ever use the word sell, just say help” right?

evidence.speaker: DM
evidence.quote: I thought of it as I had to sell something and I don’t like – I am not a salesman.

evidence.speaker: PA
evidence.quote: I don’t want to be, no offense, but I’m not an investment banking coverage guy. I’m a service provider, serving a client, you know? And the sophisticated clients will see through that if you’re just pitching and selling all the time.

caveat: Both sides describe the underlying activity almost identically — ask questions, find problems, help. Braun will even do the search-and-replace to keep a CPA firm comfortable, and Klein says selling is helping. The live disagreement is whether the word and the machinery that comes with it (process, quotas, training, accountability) should be imported or refused.

question: Should every technically strong professional be expected to build a personal book of business?

sides.position: Yes — every professional gets an origination expectation with a personal starting point and benchmarks, because without the business development piece, advancement is a struggle no matter how good the work is.

No — for a specialist whose work arrives through internal channels, chasing an external network is a measurable waste, and the individual-contributor book-of-business model is not how a firm actually grows.

why_it_matters: It determines whether a technically excellent manager is coached toward an external network and comp weighted on originations, or told to go deep internally while the firm builds a specialized growth function around them.

evidence.speaker: JR
evidence.quote: Yes, we have what we call the origination culture, which means that we have expectations for every attorney to be able to build their own book of business and we provide the tools to get them there.

evidence.speaker: AE
evidence.quote: You can be incredibly intelligent, you can offer a ton of value in what you’re able to provide but in the end of the day, if that piece is missing, it’s got to be more of a struggle.

evidence.speaker: DS
evidence.quote: With CPA firms, with accounting firms, there’s this understanding that you have to build this huge external network. Well, when you’re a specialist, you don’t really have to do that.

evidence.speaker: DS
evidence.quote: I think it really slowed my progress down by focusing on that.

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: Your banker, breakfast, lawyer, lunch, individual contributor approach toward growth, that isn’t strategic.

caveat: Swatosh is a technical specialist at a national firm where roughly 80% of his work comes from existing firm clients; Ries is describing a law firm that deliberately weights compensation on originations. Crosley is arguing about firm growth strategy rather than whether any individual should ever sell — but she is explicit that the individual-book model is the thing to replace.

question: Should you screen who gets your networking time, or meet broadly including peers, competitors and people who will never send you business?

sides.position: Screen hard — spend the time on senior people who can actually act, skip same-level peers who are competitors without authority, and decline meetings that are not a good use of a finite day.
Do not prejudge — look up, sideways and down; direct competitors can be the most useful network you have, and you take the meeting because you cannot predict where a referral comes from.

why_it_matters: A young professional at an event either works the room for gray hair or has a real conversation with the person next to them, and a firm either builds peer and competitor relationships deliberately or writes them off as unproductive.

evidence.speaker: PG
evidence.quote: You know, when you go to networking events, don’t speak to somebody that’s in the same age group as you, right? Because, if you’re 25, 20, whatever it might be, it’s very unlikely that person’s going to be able to help you, right? Because they don’t really have the authority in their own firm and also, they’re competing against you because you guys are in the same level.

evidence.speaker: MB
evidence.quote: Not every potential person who calls you to meet, given whatever profession you’re in and what your niche area is. Sometimes, it’s not the best use of your time, because you only have so much time.

evidence.speaker: TS
evidence.quote: You have to look up, sideways and down in order to have a network, because you never know who you meet today, who five years from now is going to be the key person in your community.

evidence.speaker: CM
evidence.quote: You could say that they’re not just peers, but they’re actually competitors.

evidence.speaker: EA
evidence.quote: I meet with everyone because you never know what a conversation will lead to.

caveat: Gray is advising young professionals on career access specifically, while Singer and Menary are describing mature referral and knowledge networks. Bober's screen is about volume of inbound meeting requests rather than seniority. Ackerman also rations format — she meets everyone, but not everyone in person.

question: Should business development effort go into reaching as many contacts as possible on a consistent cadence, or into a small number of deeply worked relationships and bespoke touches?

sides.position: Volume and cadence win — only one to three percent of your audience is in market at any moment, so the controlling variable is how many people you actually reach, not how well the message is crafted.
Depth wins — eighty people who will run through a wall for you beat five thousand business cards, and the right outreach is a piece of diagnostic work built for a handful of named targets a month.

why_it_matters: It is the same business development hour spent two ways: templated sends against a large list on a timer, or one researched analysis delivered to a few targets — and the two produce very different pipelines and reputations.

evidence.speaker: JV
evidence.quote: So for me, I set a looping timer for every 15 seconds and I pull up an email template. I look through it, make sure everything looks clean, personalized to the extent that I can within 15 to 20 seconds and I click the send button and I move on to the next one, right?

evidence.speaker: JV
evidence.quote: The most important criteria is, “Are you getting emails out to people?”

evidence.speaker: JH
evidence.quote: I’d rather have that 80-person army that will run through a wall for me than 5,000 business cards of people I shook their hand once at an ACG event years ago, and I can’t even remember any details about that interaction.

evidence.speaker: DL
evidence.quote: What I do is I target a couple different PE firms per month. We do something called an IP snapshot, something I innovated in the last few years with our team here.

caveat: Vawdrey is describing top-of-funnel email to a known universe of intermediaries, while Holland and LaLone are describing relationship investment and originating conversations. Drost pushes back on Holland in the episode, arguing you still need continuous new-relationship flow, much of which is one-time conversations.

question: Should a professional's business development goals include outcomes like new clients and fees, or only the inputs they directly control?

sides.position: Start from the income number you need and work backwards — new clients retained, fees collected and personal earnings belong on the same scorecard as the activity metrics.
Measuring business development on results generated is short-sighted immediate gratification against a seed-planting cycle; set goals only on what you can influence and treat outcomes as a byproduct.

why_it_matters: It changes both how an individual sets annual goals and how a firm designs incentive compensation for people whose work pays off two or three years out.

evidence.speaker: DL
evidence.quote: Once I got my N number, that is what I need to make per year to meet my financial goals, I work backwards and figure out, well, what are the things in the law practice that then allows me to reach those goals, those metrics?

evidence.speaker: MB
evidence.quote: That’s where if you’re in a professional service environment, that’s the struggle that people have, because a lot of organizations, compensation, incentive compensation is based on what results are you generating? In today’s world, it’s like immediate gratification.

evidence.speaker: PM
evidence.quote: For business development and private equity, I don’t consider success just receiving more teasers. That’s not me doing my job well because there’s no conversation then around quality, there’s no conversation around what got us an edge.

evidence.speaker: AD
evidence.quote: But don’t get yourself hooked up on only measuring something that frankly you have no influence over. Measure the stuff that if you really want to measure your BD success, measure the stuff that you have influence over.

caveat: LaLone's scorecard is mostly input metrics too — thought leadership events, trusted advisor network, five new targets a month — and Drost concedes in the episode that tracking outcomes is useful. The disagreement is whether the outcome number is a goal you are accountable to or a byproduct you merely watch.

question: Should a firm require its producers to log their relationships and interactions in a central system so business development can be analyzed and managed?

sides.position: Yes — relationship building has an empirical layer; systematize the tracking, run real analysis on the funnel, and accept that the behavior has to be forced because it will not happen on its own.

No — a producer's call notes are their own intellectual property, and the most tenured and productive people are exactly the ones who will not feed a central database, so centralize only what is volunteered and mediate the rest through human contact.

why_it_matters: A growth leader either buys and mandates a CRM and builds reporting on it, or staffs humans whose job is to extract what producers know by talking to them.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: So, I think there are a number of really empirically driven aspects of business development, and I’ll bucket them broadly in two categories.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: Then there is what I would call the more advanced side of business development or the advanced scientific side, where you’re taking some of the data and doing some real analyses

evidence.speaker: TK
evidence.quote: we know we’re not going to change the behavior unless we force it, right?

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: We don’t mandate that people put kind of all their information into a central CRM, because we found the most, let’s say, tenured and productive affiliates on the network, are the people who are least likely to want to contribute that to a central database.

caveat: Sirignano's producers are independent affiliates on a platform rather than firm employees, which weakens his ability to mandate anything — but his stated reason (top producers will not contribute) is a claim about producers generally, and Keith reports the same resistance inside partnerships while reaching the opposite conclusion.

question: Should a business owner hire a deep niche specialist, or a broad-based advisor who can see across service lines?

sides.position: Hire broad-based advisors: a professional who does one thing will steer you to that one thing whether or not it is right, so the specialist's expertise is itself a source of bias.
Specialize hard: deep niche expertise is the only thing that earns premium pricing, buyer trust and differentiation, and breadth is a positioning failure.

why_it_matters: It determines whether a firm invests in narrowing (one industry, one service line, specialist pricing) or in building a range of options and paying people to recommend outside their own lane. The same choice tells a professional whether their expertise is their strongest asset or their biggest blind spot.

evidence.speaker: SK
evidence.quote: a lot of professionals are focused upon a single area and so what they are doing is they are pushing the client towards a single solution. That single solution may or may not be the best for the client.

evidence.speaker: SK
evidence.quote: If somebody should have a restructuring, let’s do the restructuring. If I should have an operational tune-up or that’s what we should offer them. If it should be some M&A services, let’s offer it to them or let’s bring in the people who can do that and let’s set it up so that there is a financial incentive to us beyond our morality to do what is best for the client.

evidence.speaker: EW
evidence.quote: The challenge with that is that if you’re only ever a generalist, you don’t get to charge specialist pricing.

evidence.speaker: JH
evidence.quote: You are saying no to dispersing yourself, and you’re saying yes to sort of concentrating your expertise in one area, which I think compounds much faster.

evidence.speaker: MJ
evidence.quote: I don’t see people banging down the door for a full-service firm, to me is a cop-out.

caveat: Karol is arguing from the buyer's side in a period of dislocation and about strategic advice, where a wrong frame is expensive; Warren, Harrington and Jones are arguing about how a firm wins and prices recurring work. Harrington also concedes you do not need a narrow niche forever and that many broad practices were reverse-engineered from one, and Jones allows full service if it is scoped to a single industry.

question: Should a firm turn away work that does not fit its economics, or service everything that comes through a trusted referral source?

sides.position: Never refuse work because it is too small to make money on: the referral source put their reputation on the line, and declining guarantees you never see another one.
Refuse and prune deliberately: capacity is finite, and taking everything that comes through the door damages staff, margin and strategy.

why_it_matters: A listener who gets a small, unprofitable referral either services it as a relationship investment or declines it to protect capacity and staff hours. The two answers produce different client bases, different busy seasons, and different reputations with referral sources.

evidence.speaker: KM
evidence.quote: I’ve worked for companies in the past and the company’s thought process was, “Well, if it’s not big enough for us, or if it’s not – if it’s not something that we’re going to really be able to make money at, then don’t put any time into it. I’m like, “Well, that just completely ruins who I am as a human being” and I will never get another referral from that person again.

evidence.speaker: DM
evidence.quote: So our company, Forge Financial Management Consulting, we don’t take on any tax-only clients, any new tax-only clients.

evidence.speaker: DM
evidence.quote: we also want to grow in the right way and just accepting everything that comes in the door is not accomplishing that because if we accept that work and we do have that compressed time during busy season, we aren’t doing right by our staff, our team with what we set out.

evidence.speaker: JB
evidence.quote: we then decided there was some clients that we no longer, or service lines that we no longer wanted to do. We ended up selling pieces of the business. So, for instance, we did three different sales during that time of pockets of clients that didn’t fit our model anymore.

evidence.speaker: EK
evidence.quote: If you do one assist with selling a business every decade, you shouldn’t do it.

caveat: Marblestone is talking about a one-off referral from a center of influence, where the relationship is the asset; Montgomery, Bly and Kless are talking about the standing client portfolio. Marblestone would also refer the work to someone else rather than ignore it, which narrows but does not close the gap: he objects to the calculation itself, that a client is worth serving only if the engagement pays.

question: Should a professional firm replace the partnership model with a corporate structure, or design around the way partners actually behave?

sides.position: Break the partner-equals-owner model and install a corporate organizational structure with bosses, accountability and faster decisions, which is exactly what private equity brings.

Do not corporatize: the individual-book, autonomous-practitioner behavior is the nature of the business and should not be changed, and if the economics are aligned the top-down control apparatus is unnecessary.

why_it_matters: A firm leader either spends the next two years building a C-suite, reporting lines and accountability systems, or spends it aligning economics and building infrastructure around practitioners who keep running their own practices.

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: the firm breaks through the nights of the roundtable partner model and segues to the organizational structure model, because the nights of the roundtable model has served us well for a hundred years, but now, the issue is we have to have greater accountability which allows us to have greater results and faster decision-making and leadership development.

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: when you get into an organizational structure that looks more like the corporate world, which private equities are bringing into our space is that concept. Then your boss is responsible for your success, just along with you.

evidence.speaker: TK
evidence.quote: One, the partnership model, the rear current business model where a lot of the business comes rear current versus proactive, the behavior of the nature of the way people work, and which is very unique, quite frankly, it shouldn’t change.

evidence.speaker: TK
evidence.quote: You just have to remember you are a professional services firm. You don’t want to become the enterprise business.

evidence.speaker: CB
evidence.quote: We’re aligned with our principles from a financial standpoint so that we’re sharing in the net profit. So if you’re not making money, we’re not making money. As a result of being aligned in that regard, there’s not that level of top-down control that a traditional partnership has to have to make sure that people are doing the requisite amount of work at the requisite amount of quality.

caveat: Keith reaches his conclusion from technology adoption (why CRM fails in firms) rather than from governance, and he does argue for accountability structures inside practice groups. Birky's alternative is a platform of independently run practices, not a traditional partnership, so he shares Crosley's diagnosis of the practitioner-owner problem while rejecting her fix.

question: Does a mid-sized firm have to consolidate or take outside capital to stay competitive, or is independence in the middle market now the better position?

sides.position: Firms that do not transform will be the buggy whip: whether or not you take private equity money, you will be competing against private-equity-backed capability and the old model will make you irrelevant.

The merger frenzy is herd behavior: the Big Four's retreat left an enormous middle market, the capabilities firms merge to get can be bought through alliances or platforms, and staying independent is the real opportunity.

why_it_matters: This is the decision a managing partner is actually facing right now: sell to or merge into a platform, or invest to stay independent. One side says the market has already moved and delay is fatal; the other says the sellers are following each other off a cliff and abandoning the best position in the market.

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: regardless of whether you stay independent or you play in that other investment world and all the benefits that are accrued, you’re going to be competing against it. Your banker, breakfast, lawyer, lunch, individual contributor approach toward growth, that isn’t strategic. Although, not totally, because most firms have one foot in the new world and one foot in the old, but that’s not going to be good enough. You got to get both feet over into the strategic world and compete in a way where you’ve never had to compete before.

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote:
The whole neighborhood is changing and you’re going to stay there in your nice, comfortable home that you’ve been in for 50 years, 40 years, whatever, and everybody else around you has changed.
Eventually, in the market you’re going to be irrelevant.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: People have really accepted the fact that these M&As are big, some people have convinced themselves that a small firm, they can’t compete anymore, they have to get to a larger firm. There’s a lot of willing sellers today and willing buyers at the same time. That’s really what’s been feeding this real frenzy.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: Are there ways to fulfill that without merging with BDO? Yeah, there are ways. You can work with other firms.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: That’s where I think that we still have the significant opportunity is firms willing to stay in the middle market.

evidence.speaker: CB
evidence.quote: We like to look at ourselves as an alternative to that upstream merger into a traditional firm, where you become one of a couple of hundred, a couple of thousand partners, and end up being a little bit rank-and-file in terms of your leadership, and no longer run the show you used to.

caveat: Shamis is describing the accounting middle market specifically and did himself sell his firm to BDO; Crosley consults to firms on strategic growth and concedes she is not preaching that anyone should sell. The live disagreement is not about the transaction but about whether the independent mid-sized firm's position is strengthening or eroding.

question: Whose asset is the client relationship, the individual producer's or the firm's?

sides.position: The producer's: what they know about their relationships is their intellectual property, and mandating that it be centralized alienates exactly the most productive people.
The firm's: partner possessiveness about 'my clients' is a cultural obstacle to be overcome, and the firm should be talking to those clients directly.

why_it_matters: It settles whether a firm can mandate CRM entry, run its own client feedback interviews, and treat books of business as institutional assets, or whether it has to negotiate for every piece of relationship information its producers hold.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: People’s sort of knowledge about what investors are looking for in their notes from their calls, that’s their IP. So they’re going to be very strategic about how they share that.

evidence.speaker: GS
evidence.quote: We don’t mandate that people put kind of all their information into a central CRM, because we found the most, let’s say, tenured and productive affiliates on the network, are the people who are least likely to want to contribute that to a central database.

evidence.speaker: AF
evidence.quote: So that’s the first obstacle as people just simply don’t want you to ask their clients. “They’re my clients, they’re not the firm’s clients,” right? So that’s the cultural component.

caveat: Sirignano runs a broker-dealer platform of ~100 economically independent affiliates, where the relationship genuinely does belong to the affiliate; Fieldman advises CPA and law firms where partners are owners of a common enterprise. The asymmetry softens it, but Sirignano explicitly draws the parallel to CPA and law firms himself, and his prescription there is the same: mediate through human contact rather than mandate.

question: Is compliance and audit work a commodity to shed, or a franchise worth investing in?

sides.position: Get out: drop audit relationships in favor of ongoing accounting and advisory worth five to ten times the revenue, and treat today's strong compliance pricing as a temporary supply distortion that will blind you to the pivot.
Stay and invest: audit is about to expand into ESG and non-financial attestation, and breaking it out of the firm makes it more interesting, not less.

why_it_matters: A firm deciding where to put its next hire and its technology budget either converts compliance clients to advisory or builds attestation capability for a market that has not arrived yet.

evidence.speaker: EW
evidence.quote: So one of the things I say to people that have large audit practices, especially if they have clients who have really bad financials, is maybe you want to give up the idea of doing that annual audit and say, “Hey, I’d much rather help you work on your financials and your dashboards.” Just drop the ongoing audit relationship and focus on helping these guys build a better business, right?

evidence.speaker: EW
evidence.quote: you may be able to make 5 or 10 times revenue doing ongoing accounting work for this client than you’d be able to do with the audit.

evidence.speaker: CB
evidence.quote: It’s going to be very easy to get high on the hog because you’re able to command these prices at margins that are super attractive. That’s going to blind firms from what’s on the other side of that a couple of years down the road, where enough non-CPA firm players get into the business of compliance in ways that marginalize fees, compress fees, and then

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: A lot of people say, “Well, my goodness. AI is the death knell for audit.” Oh, on contrary, audit is going to incorporate ESG and we’re going to have so much non-financial statement auditing, if we do this right, that is going to be an explosion in attestation and assurance.

caveat: Warren is advising smaller firms about specific low-margin audit clients while Crosley is forecasting the profession; a large firm could act on both. But they point a firm's investment dollars in opposite directions, and Crosley's claim that separated audit becomes as exciting as advisory is the direct opposite of Birky's and Warren's premise that compliance is where value is draining away.

question: Should professionals monetize referrals with fees, or keep the exchange reciprocal?

sides.position: Take the fee from the provider: a referral service paid by the receiving firm costs the buyer nothing and is a legitimate standalone business model.
Refuse the fee and ask for a return referral instead: the cash is a trinket next to a gig that leads to more gigs.

why_it_matters: It decides whether a professional's network is a revenue line to be priced or a reciprocity system that a price would break, and whether a firm should be paying, or accepting money, for introductions at all.

evidence.speaker: LG
evidence.quote: The service providers pay me their referral fees so that’s how I make money from the transaction. It’s really no skin off the back of my private equity firm clients

evidence.speaker: TS
evidence.quote: Why would I want $500? I’d rather they refer me to my own gig, where I get a whole a whole bit. I turn down little referral fees.

caveat: Gleeman is a full-time intermediary whose entire revenue is referral fees; Singer is a professional speaker declining small fees on work he passes along. They are not choosing between the same two options, but they do disagree on the underlying claim, whether putting a price on an introduction increases or destroys its value. Sheon Karol (Ep 54) sits with Gleeman on the mechanism, arguing that only a financial incentive reliably changes who gets recommended.

question: Should growth be the default objective for a professional services firm?

sides.position: No: the profession has idolized scale, growth becomes a hungry machine the founder has to keep feeding, and 'bigger' has to answer the question better for whom.
Growth is no longer optional: cheap money is gone, passive organic growth has stopped working, and a firm that pauses demand generation to ride market conditions is exposed when they turn.

why_it_matters: In a staffing crunch a firm owner either keeps spending on demand generation because demand takes years to rebuild, or stops and asks who the growth was for. The answer also decides whether an owner reads their own exhaustion as a cost of doing business or as evidence the strategy is wrong.

evidence.speaker: DL
evidence.quote: I think there’s certainly a conversation that happens in our industry that scaling should be the objective. I don’t know if that is true. I think we have come to idolize scaling, and bigger and bigger.

evidence.speaker: DL
evidence.quote: Eventually, I think what led, for me, to a lot of the burnout that I was experiencing was a sense that I always needed to be feeding the hungry machine.

evidence.speaker: SS
evidence.quote: So for like, the last 15 years, I mean, this was for the 15 years that I ran the firm, you know, that’s what I cared about, it was the only thing I cared about was growing the firm. Grow-grow-grow. Not really sure if I knew why I was growing it besides, I want to make more money

evidence.speaker: GC
evidence.quote: It’s not going to necessarily be, let’s ride market conditions in a few years from now when conditions are poor and I look around and I haven’t invested anything. Whoops, I got a problem.

evidence.speaker: TK
evidence.quote: Now with all the changes in the market and the money not being cheap in the market anymore after COVID, it’s really hard to grow, right? Now it’s not even a choice, right?

caveat: Crosley and Keith are making a competitive-survival argument while Logan and Scarano are making an argument about purpose and personal cost, so they are not fully engaged on the same axis. They still hand a firm owner opposite instructions about whether to push growth, and Logan attacks the premise itself rather than the timing.

question: Is the case for diversity in a middle-market firm fundamentally a moral one, or is it an economic one that should be argued in investment terms?

sides.position: The argument is economic — diversity is a source of alpha and optimization, and the moral framing is actively counterproductive because it turns the work into box-ticking.
The argument is moral first — inclusion is the right thing to do, and the business benefits (better client service, more viewpoints) are additional reasons rather than the reason.

why_it_matters: It determines how a firm leader sells the initiative internally and what they do when the business case is unclear: the alpha framing says drop it where diversity doesn't improve decisions, while the moral framing says do it regardless of measured return.

evidence.speaker: LB
evidence.quote: To me, diversity is not the right thing to do. Put simply, at Palladium, we believe that diversity equals alpha.

evidence.speaker: LB
evidence.quote: I think, at the moment, too many people think that diversity is the politically correct thing to do. It’s a box-ticking exercise. I think that that leads to diverse voices not being properly included.

evidence.speaker: EL
evidence.quote: I think there are plenty of homogenous, very successful, folks, particularly financially, but like, is that optimized? No.

evidence.speaker: JB
evidence.quote: Sure. Well, fundamentally, I think it’s the right thing to do.

evidence.speaker: EL
evidence.quote: I think, be prepared, be committed to investing in a vision that’s going to go beyond just kind of a one-year approach or recent news approach. There’s a way to react to certain things and I get that. Totally get it and I’m glad about that. We’ve seen that obviously over the last year. But true alpha is generated over the long term.

caveat: Brujis and Lyles are investors arguing about portfolio and decision quality; Berggrun is a junior attorney arguing about workplace experience, and he does also cite viewpoint diversity and client service. Other guests in the same series (Charmone Adams, ep 50; Eric Gregg, ep 81) hold the 'both' middle position.

question: Should a firm set aspirational diversity targets and take bold action now, or accept that this is a slow, incremental effort with no timeline?

sides.position: Incrementalism is the failure — set aspirational targets you expect to miss and take action bold enough to reach critical mass, because a handful of diverse hires in a large firm changes nothing.
Set the intent and keep at it without a deadline — progress cannot be hypercharged, and expecting fast results is what makes firms abandon the effort.

why_it_matters: A leader building a diversity plan either commits to published, uncomfortable targets and large moves, or commits to steady intent and patience — and each side treats the other's approach as the reason nothing changes.

evidence.speaker: LB
evidence.quote: There is a good friend and mentor of mine that has this thesis that we are in a crisis of incrementalism.

evidence.speaker: LB
evidence.quote: You have to, if you have 1,000 people and you hire 10 diverse people, that’s not going to make any difference.

evidence.speaker: LB
evidence.quote: I think that, if you – you want to set aspirational targets that you know are very difficult to hit. Then if you get halfway, you’re going to be happy with the outcome.

evidence.speaker: MC
evidence.quote: It might not bear fruit right away. But over time, if you continuously have this acknowledgement that you want to build a certain team where you want to attract a certain talent, eventually, something’s going to happen.

evidence.speaker: MC
evidence.quote: I think it’s – first and foremost, having the can-do attitude, not necessarily setting a time limit and understanding that it is an ongoing effort.

evidence.speaker: JS
evidence.quote: It’s nothing that’s going to be hypercharged. It’s not going to happen in a matter of months. It’s incremental.

caveat: Sanders is answering a question about personal, relational change rather than firm hiring targets; Chao is the cleaner counterparty because she is describing her own firm's recruiting effort. Chao also runs a ~30-person PE firm where Brujis's critical-mass math works differently.

question: Do visible diversity artifacts — website committees, public statements, external certifications — do real work, or are they theater that substitutes for hiring?

sides.position: The visible artifact is load-bearing: a committee listed on a website and a Mansfield Rule certification are the only signal a candidate has before they ever interview, and they change where people apply.
Statements, calendars and stated commitments produce nothing without an actionable plan and actual hires, and claiming the value without the action does more harm than good.

why_it_matters: A firm with limited DEI capacity either invests in visible commitments that reach candidates, or treats that spend as a distraction and puts everything into hiring decisions and development.

evidence.speaker: JB
evidence.quote: Look, when I was looking at the firm and I saw that diversity and inclusion committee on its website, I didn’t know too much about the inner workings of it but more than anything, that immediately was like, “Okay, they are making an effort and I want to find out more about that”

evidence.speaker: JB
evidence.quote: That means something to the young gay law student that’s trying to figure out what firm to go to because you really don’t see many firms, at least when I was in law school 10 years ago, you don’t see diversity and inclusion or LGBT committees on every firm’s website

evidence.speaker: RG
evidence.quote: These things don’t get normalized because several organizations make that wish. They make the wish to be a more diverse organization. They don’t do the hard work of committing to creating a plan, finding the actionable items.

evidence.speaker: BH
evidence.quote: I want to be more than an aggregation of cool dates for a calendar. I want to get people hired.

evidence.speaker: LM
evidence.quote: But also, your customer will recognize whether that is a genuine and authentic effort or not. That’s where you can also burn yourself. You can do a lot more harm than you do good when you do that, right?

caveat: Berggrun concedes a website committee 'could just be like a placeholder,' and his firm pairs it with resources; the sharp disagreement is about whether the artifact is worth building before the substance exists.

question: Is the shortage of diverse professionals in middle-market finance a pipeline and awareness problem, or a problem with the hiring decisions leaders are making right now?

sides.position: The binding constraint sits upstream of the firm — candidates do not know these careers exist, and schools do not run the recruiting channels that would put them in front of firms.
The constraint is the decision maker — executives already have the power to hire, recommend and refer, and the door has to be opened by someone senior before any pipeline argument matters.

why_it_matters: It decides where a firm's effort goes: funding outreach, campus visibility and awareness programs, versus changing who is in the room for the next three hiring decisions.

evidence.speaker: RG
evidence.quote: It’s not even a glass ceiling. They don’t know that there’s even a room with that opportunity.

evidence.speaker: JB
evidence.quote: The LGBT student groups don’t have their own career fair or on-campus interviews. I think it’s a kind of an underserved group on law schools, to be frank, there’s not as many opportunities to get in front of the major firms unless you’re top in the class

evidence.speaker: BH
evidence.quote: We have enough juice to make something happen, so I’m just really committed to doing so.

evidence.speaker: BH
evidence.quote: I want to get people hired. I want to give people opportunities to get in the room, so other people in the room can meet one and see the true benefits of having a diverse workforce.

evidence.speaker: EL
evidence.quote: I would be remiss though, to also say, if I didn’t say that, it also requires someone above you, leaders above you to see beyond what they traditionally see, and to say, like, “This person can figure it out.”

evidence.speaker: MC
evidence.quote: But if you have junior positions where you can really build them up within the firm, and they have a lot of attributes that you like, and not every single one that typically checks the box, you know, take a risk with the junior ones.

caveat: Hawkins concedes he does not know how to recruit from some communities without doing it wrong, which is a pipeline-shaped problem; Grant also calls for top-down commitment. The disagreement is about which constraint binds first.

question: For an underrepresented professional, does being demonstrably excellent at the craft eventually carry you through — or does someone senior have to hand you the shot before you can prove it?

sides.position: Craft is the foundation and there is no way around it — be so good at what you do that people engage you for your value rather than your appearance, and the cultural change follows.
Working hard and being capable is not sufficient — people who work very hard in these rooms do not get the same results, so a leader has to bet on someone before the proof exists.

why_it_matters: It changes what you tell a high-potential person from a nontraditional background (grind on technical excellence vs. find an advocate) and whether a manager requires demonstrated performance before opening a new role.

evidence.speaker: CN
evidence.quote: So, I don’t think that there’s any way to get around the hard work that it takes to be valuable and important within your own industry.

evidence.speaker: CN
evidence.quote: I’m effective at what I do, which is why people want to interact with me, not necessarily of how I look.

evidence.speaker: RG
evidence.quote: And it’s easy to say work hard and you can achieve anything. That isn’t always the case. There are plenty of people that both you and I know that we see in these rooms, even these homogeneous rooms that work very hard and do not see the same results as other folks.

evidence.speaker: EL
evidence.quote: You need that leader, or leaders, managers to say, “This is what I’m valuing outside of the norm.”

evidence.speaker: MC
evidence.quote: I think a lot of organizations are saying, “I need to see someone step above and beyond in order for them to get these opportunities.” On the receiving end, it’s, “I want these opportunities, so I can show that I could step above and beyond.”

caveat: Grant appears alongside Nowaczyk in ep 41 and there endorses being good at your craft, so the disagreement is about sufficiency rather than necessity; Chao herself was required to be the best EA before being given the new role, and still argues firms should move first.

question: Outside of working hours, should you stay reachable — or hard-disconnect from email and notifications?

sides.position: Stay connected: work does not stop at five o'clock, partial connection on vacation prevents the far worse cost of falling a week behind, and the healthiest end state is a fused or integrated life rather than a defended boundary.
Disconnect deliberately: notifications off, no inbox zero, and a ritualized end-of-day shutdown, because the hours you spend not answering are worth more than the responsiveness they cost you.

why_it_matters: This decides whether a professional builds their week around availability or around protected blocks, and whether a vacation includes the phone. One side treats the disconnected hours as lost ground to be minimized; the other treats them as the input that produces the thinking clients actually pay for.

evidence.speaker: TB
evidence.quote: I can be more present on a vacation if I’m checking my email constantly. I swear to you, it’s so backwards, but honestly I could be a better person to be around if I’m doing that if I build that time in.

evidence.speaker: JH
evidence.quote: What I found is that I don’t have work life balance, I have work life fusion.

evidence.speaker: GL
evidence.quote: the reality is businesses don’t stop because it’s Friday at five o’clock at night.

evidence.speaker: DH
evidence.quote: those two hours you’re going to spend ignoring your inbox are going to do more for you than it ever could the other way around

evidence.speaker: RC
evidence.quote: whether you respond an email at 8 PM at night or 8 AM in the morning, it’s probably not going to change the outcome so much

evidence.speaker: RC
evidence.quote: It’s so easy to not shutdown at the end of the day. But your mind needs that, you need this time that is not work.

caveat: Lewis sits closest to the middle — he argues for integration but insists on a handful of genuine shutdowns a year. Hill's case for disconnection is framed as deep-work productivity rather than recovery, and Boniface describes what works for him rather than issuing a universal rule. Notably the role context does not explain the split: Hill (investment banking) and Cutter (private equity) work the same deal calendar as Boniface and Holland.

question: When you hit mid-career burnout or a job that no longer fits, should you leave — or redefine the role you are already in?

sides.position: Do not leave first: the reflex to change jobs is wrong, and the real move is telling your supervisor what you actually dislike and renegotiating your service line, niche, or role inside the firm you are in.
Staying is itself the risk: a role that does not fit you becomes a health problem and degrades everyone around you, and the mistake he names is not leaving twenty years sooner.

why_it_matters: A burned-out senior manager either books a conversation with their partner about changing what they work on, or starts a search. Crabtree and Daly say the search is a false exit that will not cure anything; Marblestone says pricing risk only financially is what keeps people in seats that are costing them their health.

evidence.speaker: RC
evidence.quote: I think the first reaction most people have is, “I got to change jobs.” That’s not necessarily what you need to do.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: That is a false choice and it took me a long time to realize that

evidence.speaker: KM
evidence.quote: I also looked at risk. When I worked at a large corporation last, I looked at risk as, if I stay here, it’s going to create a health problem for me.

evidence.speaker: KM
evidence.quote: I wish I had taken the initiative to do something different 20 years ago.

caveat: Marblestone's misfit was structural — corporate politics at a large company, late in a long career — while Crabtree and Daly are describing workload and service-line burnout inside professional firms. Both sides allow the other move eventually: Crabtree did step out of the managing partner role and Daly did relocate; the disagreement is over whether leaving is the first response or the last one. Speaker label 'SM' is the transcript's tag for Erik Daly.

question: Under real pressure, should a leader project calm they do not feel, or let their people see the strain?

sides.position: Bring calm even while screaming inside — fake it till you make it, because hundreds of people are counting on you to figure it out, and the fear goes home with you, not to the team.
Visible imperfection is the job: leaders have to be openly wrong and vulnerable for their people to be, and hiding your actual state degrades the very judgment everyone is depending on.

why_it_matters: On the morning a deal collapses or a downturn hits, the leader either walks in composed and absorbs it privately or says out loud that they are struggling. One side believes the composure is what keeps the organization functioning; the other believes concealment costs both connection and decision quality.

evidence.speaker: SBB
evidence.quote: But it’s bringing a sense of calm, even if you’re screaming inside.

evidence.speaker: SBB
evidence.quote: You got to fake it till you make it. Because you’ve got sometimes tens, hundreds, thousands of people counting on you to figure it out.

evidence.speaker: BV
evidence.quote: People that lead have to be okay with not being perfect and being perfect – I mean, being imperfect, making mistakes, being vulnerable allows you to better connect with people.

evidence.speaker: SM
evidence.quote: if you try to hide from those things, it’ll deteriorate your ability to make sound decisions

caveat: Black-Beth prescribes the calm specifically for acute crisis with jobs at stake, and says elsewhere in the same episode that on an ordinary challenging day her team will know if it affects the work. Vance is describing steady-state team leadership and Daly is describing personal mental health rather than crisis command — but Daly's claim is precisely that concealment is what damages the decisions a leader is being trusted to make. Speaker label 'SM' is the transcript's tag for Erik Daly.

question: Is there a right personal routine to build — protected morning practice before work — or does the standard template need to be inverted for the person you actually are?

sides.position: Growth is a muscle you exercise on a schedule: get up early, take the quiet time before you log on, journal daily, and do it especially on the days you do not feel like it.

There is no one size fits all: the wake-early-and-work-out-first template failed him because his mind was already in his inbox, and the fix was inverting it — hard work at the desk first, training after.

why_it_matters: A professional whose morning routine keeps collapsing either concludes they need more discipline about the prescribed sequence, or concludes the sequence itself is wrong for them and rebuilds it backwards. Alberts also argues that watching other people's routines on LinkedIn actively obstructs finding your own.

evidence.speaker: BD
evidence.quote: To me, growth is like a muscle. You have to exercise it.

evidence.speaker: BD
evidence.quote: whether it’s me where I get up early and spend my mornings, just that quiet time, that time to think, that time to prepare for your day

evidence.speaker: BD
evidence.quote: I still write by hand in a journal every morning.

evidence.speaker: MA
evidence.quote: I’ve read plenty of books and what I’ve found is there’s really no one size fits all.

evidence.speaker: MA
evidence.quote: So, I sort of shifted and said, “Okay, maybe I’m still waking up at 5 AM. But I’m taking a cup of coffee, and I’m getting at my desk and maybe knocking out some work first.”

caveat: Both value consistency and both in fact run a morning practice — Alberts keeps gratitude and reading, he just moved work ahead of the workout. The live disagreement is whether the sequence is prescribable at all, and Doyle does concede that everyone 'finds their outlet.' Alberts also cuts against the measurement instinct: a week of 30-minute time tracking cost him 30 minutes a day.

question: Does being authentic mean being the same person in every room, or adapting how you present to the room you are in?

sides.position: Same person everywhere: authenticity is consistency of behavior across contexts, and trying to fit into a stiff, buttoned-up box costs you the memorability that is the entire point.

Modifying how you communicate across audiences — code switching — is essential to navigating corporate America and is now an act of respect that coexists with authenticity rather than contradicting it.

why_it_matters: Walking into a board meeting or a client dinner, a professional either holds their register constant on principle or deliberately shifts it. Holland and Ackerman would read the shift as inauthentic acting; Adams reads the refusal to shift as a failure of respect and, for people of color, a real career cost.

evidence.speaker: JH
evidence.quote: you’re the same person at a work function, that you are in your backyard hosting someone for a barbecue, you’re the same person in front of your children and not in front of your children.

evidence.speaker: EA
evidence.quote: I also am not trying to fit into a box and be this stiff, buttoned-up person. I’m not that way. I am professional, but I am authentically me

evidence.speaker: CA
evidence.quote: And what code switching is, is essentially learning how to interact with different people. But more importantly, changing or modifying how you approach, how you communicate

evidence.speaker: CA
evidence.quote: I think when you merge the two being authentic, and then the code-switching element is really the understanding of the dynamics of respect.

caveat: Sharp context asymmetry: Adams is a Black professional describing what navigating predominantly white corporate spaces has required since the Civil Rights era, while Holland and Ackerman are describing a consistency that costs them nothing. They would still disagree given the same context — Adams argues the modern version is about respect and applies generally, and his example is choosing jazz over rap in a board meeting. Jamil Sanders (ep 39) lands explicitly between them, arguing for a negotiated middle rather than either pole.
